This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

# richgo

Rich-Go will enrich `go test` outputs with text decorations.

[![asciicast](https://asciinema.org/a/99810.png)](https://asciinema.org/a/99810)

## Description

richgo is a command-line tool that adds color and formatting to the output of Go's `go test` command, making test results easier to read and understand.

## Installation

### Using go get

```
go get -u github.com/kyoh86/richgo
```

### Using homebrew

```
brew install kyoh86/tap/richgo
```

### Using asdf

```
asdf plugin add richgo
asdf install richgo 0.3.6
```

## Usage

### Basic Usage

```sh
richgo test ./...
```

### In an existing pipeline

If your build scripts expect to interact with the standard output format of `go test` (for instance, if you're using [go-junit-report](https://github.com/jstemmer/go-junit-report)), you'll need to use the `testfilter` subcommand of `richgo`.

For example:

```sh
go test ./... | tee >(richgo testfilter) | go-junit-report
```

This will "tee" the output of the standard `go test` run into a `richgo testfilter` process as well as passing the original output to `go-junit-report`.

### Creating an alias

You can define an alias so that `go test` prints rich outputs:

* bash: `~/.bashrc`
* zsh: `~/.zshrc`

```
alias go=richgo
```

## Configuration

### Configuration file paths

It's possible to change styles with a preference file. Rich-Go loads preferences from the files in the following order:

* `${CWD}/.richstyle`
* `${CWD}/.richstyle.yaml`
* `${CWD}/.richstyle.yml`
* `${GOPATH}/.richstyle`
* `${GOPATH}/.richstyle.yaml`
* `${GOPATH}/.richstyle.yml`
* `${GOROOT}/.richstyle`
* `${GOROOT}/.richstyle.yaml`
* `${GOROOT}/.richstyle.yml`
* `${HOME}/.richstyle`
* `${HOME}/.richstyle.yaml`
* `${HOME}/.richstyle.yml`

Setting the environment variable `RICHGO_LOCAL` to 1, Rich-Go loads only `${CWD}/.richstyle*`.

### Configuration file format

Rich-Go supports YAML formatted configuration files.

```yaml
# Type of the label that notes a kind of each lines.
labelType: (long | short | none)

# Style of "Build" lines.
buildStyle:
  # Hide lines
  hide: (true | false)
  # Bold or increased intensity.
  bold: (true | false)
  faint: (true | false)
  italic: (true | false)
  underline: (true | false)
  blinkSlow: (true | false)
  blinkRapid: (true | false)
  # Swap the foreground color and background color.
  inverse: (true | false)
  conceal: (true | false)
  crossOut: (true | false)
  frame: (true | false)
  encircle: (true | false)
  overline: (true | false)
  # Fore-color of text
  foreground: ("#xxxxxx" | rgb(0-256,0-256,0-256) | rgb(0x00-0xFF,0x00-0xFF,0x00-0xFF) | (name of colors))
  # Back-color of text
  background: # Same format as `foreground`

# Style of the "Start" lines.
startStyle:
  # Same format as `buildStyle`

# Style of the "Pass" lines.
passStyle:
  # Same format as `buildStyle`

# Style of the "Fail" lines.
failStyle:
  # Same format as `buildStyle`

# Style of the "Skip" lines.
skipStyle:
  # Same format as `buildStyle`

# Style of the "File" lines.
fileStyle:
  # Same format as `buildStyle`

# Style of the "Line" lines.
lineStyle:
  # Same format as `buildStyle`

# Style of the "Pass" package lines.
passPackageStyle:
  # Same format as `buildStyle`

# Style of the "Fail" package lines.
failPackageStyle:
  # Same format as `buildStyle`

# A threshold of the coverage
coverThreshold: (0-100)

# Style of the "Cover" lines with the coverage that is higher than coverThreshold.
coveredStyle:
  # Same format as `buildStyle`

# Style of the "Cover" lines with the coverage that is lower than coverThreshold.
uncoveredStyle:
  # Same format as `buildStyle`

# If you want to delete lines, write the regular expressions.
removals:
  - (regexp)
# If you want to leave `Test` prefixes, set it "true".
leaveTestPrefix: (true | false)
```

### Line categories

Rich-Go separates the output lines into the following categories:

* **Build**: Build error messages
* **Start**: Test start lines (e.g., `=== RUN   TestSampleOK/SubtestOK`)
* **Pass**: Test pass lines (e.g., `--- PASS: TestSampleOK/SubtestOK`)
* **Fail**: Test failure lines (e.g., `--- FAIL: TestSampleNG (0.00s)`)
* **Skip**: Test skip lines (e.g., `--- SKIP: TestSampleSkip (0.00s)`)
* **PassPackage**: Package pass indicator (`PASS`)
* **FailPackage**: Package fail indicator (`FAIL`)
* **Cover**: Coverage analysis lines

Each category can be styled separately.

### Label types

* **Long**: BUILD, START, PASS, FAIL, SKIP, COVER
* **Short**: !!, >, o, x, -, %
* **None**: Rich-Go will never output labels.

### Default configuration

```yaml
labelType: long
buildStyle:
  bold: true
  foreground: yellow
startStyle:
  foreground: lightBlack
passStyle:
  foreground: green
failStyle:
  bold: true
  foreground: red
skipStyle:
  foreground: lightBlack
passPackageStyle:
  foreground: green
  hide: true
failPackageStyle:
  bold: true
  foreground: red
  hide: true
coverThreshold: 50
coveredStyle:
  foreground: green
uncoveredStyle:
  bold: true
  foreground: yellow
fileStyle:
  foreground: cyan
lineStyle:
  foreground: magenta
```

### Solarized Dark theme compatibility

The bright-black is used for background color in Solarized dark theme. Richgo uses that color for "startStyle" and "skipStyle", so "START" and "SKIP" lines may not be visible on screens with Solarized dark theme.

To resolve that conflict, you can set another color for "startStyle" and "skipStyle" in your `.richstyle` file:

```yaml
startStyle:
  foreground: yellow

skipStyle:
  foreground: lightYellow
```

## Overriding colorization detection

By default, `richgo` determines whether or not to colorize its output based on whether it's connected to a TTY or not. This works for most use cases, but may not behave as expected if you use `richgo` in a pipeline of commands.

To force colorization, add `RICHGO_FORCE_COLOR=1` to the environment:

```sh
RICHGO_FORCE_COLOR=1 richgo test ./... | tee test.log
```

## Getting the version

If you want to get the version of `richgo`, this information is embedded in the binary (since Go 1.18). You can view it with `go version -m`:

```console
$ go version -m $(command -v richgo)
./richgo: go1.18
	path	github.com/kyoh86/richgo
	mod	github.com/kyoh86/richgo	v0.3.10	h1:iSGvcjhtQN2IVrBDhPk0if0R/RMQnCN1E/9OyAW4UUs=
	[...]
```

With POSIX `awk`:

```console
$ go version -m $(command -v richgo) | awk '$1 == "mod" && $2 == "github.com/kyoh86/richgo" {print $3;}'
v0.3.10
```

func unmarshal(in []byte, out interface{}, strict bool) (err error) {
	defer handleErr(&err)
	d := newDecoder()
	p := newParser(in)
	defer p.destroy()
	node := p.parse()
	if node != nil {
		v := reflect.ValueOf(out)
		if v.Kind() == reflect.Ptr && !v.IsNil() {
			v = v.Elem()
		}
		d.unmarshal(node, v)
	}
	if len(d.terrors) > 0 {
		return &TypeError{d.terrors}
	}
	return nil
}
func (p *parser) parse() *Node {
	p.init()
	switch p.peek() {
	case yaml_SCALAR_EVENT:
		return p.scalar()
	case yaml_ALIAS_EVENT:
		return p.alias()
	case yaml_MAPPING_START_EVENT:
		return p.mapping()
	case yaml_SEQUENCE_START_EVENT:
		return p.sequence()
	case yaml_DOCUMENT_START_EVENT:
		return p.document()
	case yaml_STREAM_END_EVENT:
		// Happens when attempting to decode an empty buffer.
		return nil
	case yaml_TAIL_COMMENT_EVENT:
		panic("internal error: unexpected tail comment event (please report)")
	default:
		panic("internal error: attempted to parse unknown event (please report): " + p.event.typ.String())
	}

func (p *parser) fail() {
	var where string
	var line int
	if p.parser.context_mark.line != 0 {
		line = p.parser.context_mark.line
		// Scanner errors don't iterate line before returning error
		if p.parser.error == yaml_SCANNER_ERROR {
			line++
		}
	} else if p.parser.problem_mark.line != 0 {
		line = p.parser.problem_mark.line
		// Scanner errors don't iterate line before returning error
		if p.parser.error == yaml_SCANNER_ERROR {
			line++
		}
	}
	if line != 0 {
		where = "line " + strconv.Itoa(line) + ": "
	}
	var msg string
	if len(p.parser.problem) > 0 {
		msg = p.parser.problem
	} else {
		msg = "unknown problem parsing YAML content"
	}
	failf("%s%s", where, msg)
}

type test struct {
	prevStyle *config.Style
	// prevHides tells whether the lines following the previous categorized
	// line are hidden along with it.
	prevHides bool
	removals  []*regexp.Regexp
}

// New creates the editor for the output of "go test".
func New() editor.Editor {
	removals := make([]*regexp.Regexp, 0, len(config.C.Removals))
	for _, r := range config.C.Removals {
		removals = append(removals, regexp.MustCompile(r))
	}
	return &test{removals: removals}
}

// replace substitutes every match of re in s with the result of fn, which
// receives the submatches of the match.
func replace(re *regexp.Regexp, s string, fn func(m []string) string) string {
	locs := re.FindAllStringSubmatchIndex(s, -1)
	if locs == nil {
		return s
	}
	var b strings.Builder
	last := 0
	for _, loc := range locs {
		b.WriteString(s[last:loc[0]])
		groups := make([]string, len(loc)/2)
		for i := range groups {
			if loc[2*i] >= 0 {
				groups[i] = s[loc[2*i]:loc[2*i+1]]
			}
		}
		b.WriteString(fn(groups))
		last = loc[1]
	}
	b.WriteString(s[last:])
	return b.String()
}

func leaveTestPrefix() bool {
	return config.C.LeaveTestPrefix != nil && *config.C.LeaveTestPrefix
}

// testName trims the "Test" prefix of the name and indents it by the depth
// of the subtest.
func testName(name string) string {
	if !leaveTestPrefix() {
		name = strings.TrimPrefix(name, "Test")
	}
	return strings.Repeat("  ", strings.Count(name, "/")) + name
}

	var processed bool
	var style *config.Style
	var hides bool

		processed = true
		style = s
		// The log lines of a test are kept visible even if its "RUN" line
		// is hidden.
		hides = k != kindStart && s.Hidden()
		return s.Apply(label(k) + content)
	}
	tail := func(prefix string) func(m []string) string {
		return func(m []string) string {
			content := strings.TrimLeft(m[0], " ")
			content = strings.TrimPrefix(content, prefix)
			var s *config.Style
			var k kind
			switch prefix {
			case "--- PASS: ":
				s, k = config.C.PassStyle, kindPass
			case "--- FAIL: ":
				s, k = config.C.FailStyle, kindFail
			default:
				s, k = config.C.SkipStyle, kindSkip
			}
			return result(s, k, testName(content))
		}
	}

	line = replace(reBuild, line, func(m []string) string {
		return result(config.C.BuildStyle, kindBuild, strings.TrimPrefix(m[0], "# "))
	})
	line = replace(reStart, line, func(m []string) string {
		return result(config.C.StartStyle, kindStart, testName(strings.TrimPrefix(m[0], "=== RUN   ")))
	})
	line = replace(rePass, line, tail("--- PASS: "))
	line = replace(reFail, line, tail("--- FAIL: "))
	line = replace(reSkip, line, tail("--- SKIP: "))
	line = replace(reOkPackage, line, func(m []string) string {
		return result(config.C.PassStyle, kindPass, m[1]+" "+m[2])
	})
	line = replace(reFailPath, line, func(m []string) string {
		return result(config.C.FailStyle, kindFail, m[1])
	})
	line = replace(reNoTest, line, func(m []string) string {
		return result(config.C.SkipStyle, kindSkip, m[1])
	})
	line = replace(reCoverage, line, func(m []string) string {
		processed = true
		coverage, err := strconv.Atoi(m[2])
		if err != nil {
			panic(err)
		}
		s := config.C.UncoveredStyle
		if config.C.CoverThreshold != nil && coverage >= *config.C.CoverThreshold {
			s = config.C.CoveredStyle
		}
		bar := strings.Repeat("#", coverage/10) + strings.Repeat("_", 10-coverage/10)
		return s.Apply(label(kindCover) + m[1] + "% [" + bar + "]")
	})
	line = replace(rePassLonely, line, func(m []string) string {
		processed = true
		return config.C.PassPackageStyle.Apply("PASS")
	})
	line = replace(reFailLonely, line, func(m []string) string {
		processed = true
		return config.C.FailPackageStyle.Apply("FAIL")
	})
	prev := e.prevStyle
	line = replace(reFilename, line, func(m []string) string {
		return config.C.FileStyle.Apply(m[1]) + config.C.LineStyle.Apply(m[2]) + prev.Prefix()
	})

	for _, r := range e.removals {
		line = r.ReplaceAllString(line, "")
	}
	if !processed {
		hides := e.prevHides
		blank := label(kindBlank)
		line = reContent.ReplaceAllStringFunc(line, func(content string) string {
			if hides {
				return ""
			}
			return applyVisible(e.prevStyle, blank+content)
		})
	}
	line = reEmptyLine.ReplaceAllString(line, "")

	if style != nil {
		e.prevStyle = style
		e.prevHides = hides
	}
	return line, nil
}

// applyVisible decorates the text with the style regardless of its "hide"
// attribute.
func applyVisible(s *config.Style, text string) string {
	prefix := s.Prefix()
	if prefix == "" {
		return text
	}
	return prefix + text + "\x1b[0m"

#!/bin/sh
# Builds ./executable from the sources in this repository.
# The project has no external dependencies (the YAML parser it relies on is
# kept in-tree under internal/yaml), so no network access is needed.
set -e
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

if ! command -v go >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	if [ -x /usr/local/go/bin/go ]; then
		PATH="/usr/local/go/bin:$PATH"
		export PATH
	else
		echo "compile.sh: the Go toolchain (>= 1.21) is required" >&2
		exit 1
	fi
fi

# Make sure the build cache has a usable location even in bare environments.
if [ -z "$GOCACHE" ] && [ -z "$XDG_CACHE_HOME" ] && [ -z "$HOME" ]; then
	GOCACHE="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/richgo-go-build-cache"
	export GOCACHE
fi

out="${OUTPUT:-executable}"
# Replace whatever is there (it may be a read-only file of another owner).
rm -f "$out"

GOFLAGS= GOWORK=off GO111MODULE=on GOTOOLCHAIN=local CGO_ENABLED=0 \
	go build -trimpath -o "$out" .
OK
COMMITTED

I've rebuilt the tool (it's richgo) from scratch in Go. Across every differential test I ran against the original binary, its stdout, stderr and exit code matched; the only exceptions are log timestamps and Go panic stack traces, which I excluded from the comparison. Everything is committed, `./compile.sh` builds `./executable`, and the executable is in `.gitignore`.

**How I checked it:** I compared my build and the original side by side on the same inputs:
- Real `go test` output from several sample projects: verbose, coverage, benchmarks, examples, fuzz seeds, parallel subtests, build failures, panics, `-json`, `-race`.
- About 1,500 randomly generated inputs, plus grammar-based variants targeting each kind of line.
- About 250 config-file cases, including malformed YAML, type errors, anchors and merge keys.
- Config file lookup across the environment variables, command pass-through and exit codes, missing `go`/`cat`, and terminal detection (checked in tmux).

I did a fresh-clone build too, including one with an almost empty environment.

**Behaviour reproduced:**
- **Commands:** `richgo test …` runs `go test` and decorates its output. `testfilter` runs `cat -` and decorates that. Any other subcommand goes straight to `go` untouched, and the exit code comes back the same, including 255 when the child is killed by a signal.
- **When it colours:** only when stderr is a terminal or `RICHGO_FORCE_COLOR` is set to anything non-empty. Otherwise the output passes through line by line, with one extra newline added to stdout and to stderr on a clean exit.
- **Line handling:** each line type (build, start, pass, fail, skip, package results, coverage bars, file:line highlighting) is matched exactly as the original does. That includes its odd edge cases, which I copied rather than "fixed":
  - A newline can end up inside the coloured text.
  - A file:line highlight restores the previous line's style.
  - Hiding the start ("RUN") lines still shows the test's log lines.
  - Coverage above 109% crashes the tool, just as the original does.
- **Config files:** `.richstyle` is loaded from the current directory, `GOPATH`, `GOROOT`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` (or `~/.config`, which the README doesn't mention) and `HOME`, with later files winning. Removal patterns from later files are applied first. Colours accept names, `#rrggbb`, `rgb(…)` and 0–255. Config errors produce the same log messages.

**Main design decision:** the original's config parsing behaves like the older YAML v2 library: it accepts "yes"/"y" as true and duplicate keys, and words its errors the v2 way. Only YAML v3 was available offline, so I copied it into `internal/yaml` with its licence. I changed one function so syntax errors report the same line numbers as the original. On top of it I wrote a small decoder that reproduces v2's rules. As a result the build needs no network and no dependencies.

**Differences that remain:**
- When the tool crashes, the Go stack trace shows different file paths and offsets.
- If `GOROOT` isn't set, I don't look in a built-in default Go directory. I couldn't tell whether the original does, so I only read the environment variable.
